questions: Of ten real data scientist postings you would apply to, how many state a master's as required rather than preferred?
Does the certificate cover the depth you would need, such as statistics, machine learning and a capstone project, or only introductory material?
What is your impression that job ads require a master's based on: how many ads you have actually read, and which companies?
Which kinds of data roles fit mechanical engineers best, such as simulation, manufacturing analytics or test data, and do they ask for a master's?
What share of the master's graduates who changed careers had a data science job within six months, and how many of the certificate's graduates did?
Is there a data, analytics or simulation team at your current employer that you could move to or collaborate with?
What are the application deadlines for the master's, and what does waiting one more year cost you?
At what monthly spending level and savings balance would full-time study stop being workable for you?
How many hours a week could you realistically study next to your current job, and what in your week would give way?
What evidence do you have that graduates of this well-known program get offers within two years of starting, as opposed to just being well known?

criteria: Likelihood of landing a data science role within 2 years, tested against actual job requirements and what hiring managers accept
Ability to show skills through projects, portfolio or applied work that employers value
Financial position through the 2 years, including tuition, lost income and savings runway
Fit with existing mechanical engineering experience, such as a path through current employer or domain-specific data roles
stated_facts: Currently works as a mechanical design engineer
Goal: move into a data science role within 2 years
No other income during full-time study
Job ads for data scientists often list a master's degree
The master's program is well known
The certificate is cheaper and flexible

assumptions.text: A master's degree is required for the kind of data science roles the user wants, even though ads only often list it.
The well-known program will translate into job offers within the 2 years.
A part-time certificate while working will not be taken seriously enough, or will not give enough depth.
The user can fund and manage living costs through full-time study, or the workload of part-time study alongside the job.

uncertainties.text: Do the actual target employers and roles (including data roles within mechanical or engineering industries) require a master's, or do they hire on demonstrated skills and projects?
uncertainties.if_resolved: If most target roles filter on a master's, the full-time master's is favored; if portfolio and domain skills are accepted, the certificate is favored.

uncertainties.text: Is there an internal route: can the user move into data-related work at the current employer, using engineering domain knowledge, while studying part-time?
uncertainties.if_resolved: If an internal transition is available, keeping the job with the certificate is favored; if not, the master's with its recruiting networks may be favored.

uncertainties.text: What does the master's cost in total (tuition, living costs, lost salary), how long are savings sufficient, and can the user afford a lost 1 to 2 years of income?
uncertainties.if_resolved: If savings or funding cover it comfortably, the master's is feasible; if it leads to debt or strain, the certificate is favored.

uncertainties.text: What are the programs' outcomes: placement rates, internships, career services, alumni networks, and the certificate's depth, projects and employer recognition?
uncertainties.if_resolved: If the master's has strong placement for career changers, it is favored; if certificate graduates also get hired, its lower cost favors it.

uncertainties.text: Can the user realistically carry a part-time program on top of a full-time job (hours, employer flexibility, energy), and does the user already have the math, statistics and programming background?
uncertainties.if_resolved: If capacity and background are good, the certificate is favored; if the workload is unmanageable or the background is weak, the structured full-time master's is favored.

uncertainties.text: Does the admission timeline and the current job market for entry-level data scientists, which is competitive, fit within the 2-year goal?
uncertainties.if_resolved: If the market is hiring entry-level career changers, either path can work and cost decides; if it is tight, the master's credential and networks may matter more.

chosen.question: Of ten real data scientist postings you would apply to, how many state a master's as required rather than preferred?
chosen.why: If most make it a hard filter, the master's gains a clear edge; if few do, the certificate does.
chosen.answer_path: Collect 10 to 15 current postings from your target employers and tally required versus preferred degree wording.

chosen.question: Does the certificate cover the depth you would need, such as statistics, machine learning and a capstone project, or only introductory material?
chosen.why: Checks whether the depth concern is true for this certificate.
chosen.answer_path: Read the syllabus, sample assignments and capstone descriptions, and ask for alumni projects.

chosen.question: What is your impression that job ads require a master's based on: how many ads you have actually read, and which companies?
chosen.why: Checks the sample behind your belief.
chosen.answer_path: Count the ads you have looked at and compare with a systematic sample.

chosen.question: Which kinds of data roles fit mechanical engineers best, such as simulation, manufacturing analytics or test data, and do they ask for a master's?
chosen.why: Adjacent roles may be easier to reach than general data science.
chosen.answer_path: Search job boards for analytics roles in engineering industries and note requirements.

chosen.question: What share of the master's graduates who changed careers had a data science job within six months, and how many of the certificate's graduates did?
chosen.why: Placement for people like you separates the two options more directly than reputation does.
chosen.answer_path: Ask both programs for outcome reports, and check graduate profiles on LinkedIn.

chosen.question: Is there a data, analytics or simulation team at your current employer that you could move to or collaborate with?
chosen.why: An internal route would make the part-time path clearly stronger.
chosen.answer_path: Check internal job boards and org charts, and ask your manager or a contact in the analytics team.

chosen.question: What are the application deadlines for the master's, and what does waiting one more year cost you?
chosen.why: Identifies the real deadline and the cost of delay.
chosen.answer_path: Check admission calendars and ask the program whether later intakes exist.

chosen.question: At what monthly spending level and savings balance would full-time study stop being workable for you?
chosen.why: Sets the money threshold for the master's.
chosen.answer_path: List fixed monthly costs, compute months of runway at your savings, and decide your minimum reserve.

chosen.question: How many hours a week could you realistically study next to your current job, and what in your week would give way?
chosen.why: Checks whether the part-time load is manageable.
chosen.answer_path: Track a typical week of hours, add the program's stated weekly workload, and ask current part-time students.

chosen.question: What evidence do you have that graduates of this well-known program get offers within two years of starting, as opposed to just being well known?
chosen.why: Reputation does not guarantee offers in your timeframe.
chosen.answer_path: Look for placement statistics, employer lists and alumni outcomes for the specific cohort years.

candidates.question: Of ten real data scientist postings you would apply to, how many state a master's as required rather than preferred?
candidates.why: If most make it a hard filter, the master's gains a clear edge; if few do, the certificate does.
candidates.answer_path: Collect 10 to 15 current postings from your target employers and tally required versus preferred degree wording.

candidates.question: Do data scientists who moved over from mechanical or other engineering fields at your target companies hold a master's, or did they come in through projects and domain knowledge?
candidates.why: Shows which path career changers like you actually took into those roles.
candidates.answer_path: Search LinkedIn for people with a mechanical engineering background now in data roles and check their education; message two or three of them.

candidates.question: Is there a data, analytics or simulation team at your current employer that you could move to or collaborate with?
candidates.why: An internal route would make the part-time path clearly stronger.
candidates.answer_path: Check internal job boards and org charts, and ask your manager or a contact in the analytics team.

candidates.question: What would the master's cost you in total, counting tuition, living costs and the salary you give up, and how many months can your savings cover that?
candidates.why: If the total cannot be covered without debt, the full-time route loses clearly.
candidates.answer_path: Get the tuition schedule from the program, add your monthly expenses, and compare with your savings and notice-period terms.

candidates.question: What share of the master's graduates who changed careers had a data science job within six months, and how many of the certificate's graduates did?
candidates.why: Placement for people like you separates the two options more directly than reputation does.
candidates.answer_path: Ask both programs for outcome reports, and check graduate profiles on LinkedIn.

candidates.question: Have you seen any data science role you want where the company has actually turned down someone without a master's?
candidates.why: Checks whether the master's is really required or only often listed.
candidates.answer_path: Ask recruiters, hiring managers or recent hires at target companies whether the degree is a hard filter.

candidates.question: What evidence do you have that graduates of this well-known program get offers within two years of starting, as opposed to just being well known?
candidates.why: Reputation does not guarantee offers in your timeframe.
candidates.answer_path: Look for placement statistics, employer lists and alumni outcomes for the specific cohort years.

candidates.question: Which employers or hiring managers have told you, or shown through hires, that they would discount a part-time online certificate?
candidates.why: Tests the belief that the certificate would not be taken seriously.
candidates.answer_path: Ask people who hire data scientists, and look at whether your target firms have hired certificate-holders.

candidates.question: Does the certificate cover the depth you would need, such as statistics, machine learning and a capstone project, or only introductory material?
candidates.why: Checks whether the depth concern is true for this certificate.
candidates.answer_path: Read the syllabus, sample assignments and capstone descriptions, and ask for alumni projects.

candidates.question: How many hours a week could you realistically study next to your current job, and what in your week would give way?
candidates.why: Checks whether the part-time load is manageable.
candidates.answer_path: Track a typical week of hours, add the program's stated weekly workload, and ask current part-time students.

candidates.question: Does the master's actually put career changers in front of employers, for example through internships, recruiting events or alumni referrals, in a way you could not replicate yourself?
candidates.why: Tests the link between the degree and access to jobs.
candidates.answer_path: Ask the program for the list of recruiting partners and internship placements, and speak to two alumni.

candidates.question: If you finished the certificate and built three solid projects, would the people who screen applications for your target roles pass you through?
candidates.why: Tests whether skills evidence can replace the degree in the screening step.
candidates.answer_path: Ask recruiters or data team leads to review a sample portfolio and say how it would be screened.

candidates.question: Does working while studying help your job search, for example by letting you use data work at your employer as portfolio material?
candidates.why: Tests whether keeping the job adds to the transition, beyond income.
candidates.answer_path: Look at your current work for data-heavy tasks and ask your manager if you can take some on.

candidates.question: Do the projects you would complete in each program produce work an employer could see and judge, such as public repositories or case studies?
candidates.why: Tests the link from program to visible evidence of skill.
candidates.answer_path: Review the project requirements of both programs and sample student portfolios.

candidates.question: Does the master's timeline, from application to graduation, leave you enough months to job-search before the two-year mark?
candidates.why: Tests whether the degree can deliver the goal in the time you set.
candidates.answer_path: Check application deadlines, program length and when graduates typically start job searching.

candidates.question: At what monthly spending level and savings balance would full-time study stop being workable for you?
candidates.why: Sets the money threshold for the master's.
candidates.answer_path: List fixed monthly costs, compute months of runway at your savings, and decide your minimum reserve.

candidates.question: How many weeks of overtime, travel or project deadlines at your job would make part-time study stop working?
candidates.why: Finds when the certificate path breaks down under job load.
candidates.answer_path: Review your last year's peak periods and ask your manager about expected workload.

candidates.question: If the entry-level market is still weak when you finish, how many extra months of searching could you afford under each option?
candidates.why: Sets the time limit past which each option fails.
candidates.answer_path: Estimate your extra runway after study ends, and check current time-to-hire for junior data roles.

candidates.question: What math, statistics and programming do you need before the master's or certificate starts, and how long would catching up take if you lack it?
candidates.why: A weak background can make either option take longer than planned.
candidates.answer_path: Compare the program prerequisites with your skills, and try a placement or sample course.

candidates.question: If your employer would not allow reduced hours or time for study, would the certificate still be workable?
candidates.why: Employer flexibility may limit the part-time path.
candidates.answer_path: Ask your manager and HR about schedule flexibility and any study support.

candidates.question: Is there a third route, such as a short bootcamp, a self-study plan with projects, or a part-time master's, that you have not weighed?
candidates.why: The map only covers the two options.
candidates.answer_path: Look up part-time or online master's programs and compare them with your two choices.

candidates.question: Which kinds of data roles fit mechanical engineers best, such as simulation, manufacturing analytics or test data, and do they ask for a master's?
candidates.why: Adjacent roles may be easier to reach than general data science.
candidates.answer_path: Search job boards for analytics roles in engineering industries and note requirements.

candidates.question: Do any scholarships, employer sponsorship or student work options exist that would change the cost of the master's?
candidates.why: Funding could change the financial picture.
candidates.answer_path: Ask the program's admissions and financial aid offices, and ask HR about tuition support.

candidates.question: What visa or location limits, if any, apply to the roles you want, and do they favor a local degree?
candidates.why: Location and work-permit rules may affect which credential matters.
candidates.answer_path: Check job posting location and work authorization requirements, and ask the program about graduate work rights.

candidates.question: Would you enjoy the day-to-day work of a data scientist enough to commit, and have you tried a small real data project to find out?
candidates.why: A sample of the work could change whether either option is worth it.
candidates.answer_path: Spend a few weekends on a real dataset from your own work and note what you liked.

candidates.question: Which choice is harder to reverse: quitting your job for a full-time master's, or spending a year on a certificate and finding it was not enough?
candidates.why: Shows which mistake is more expensive to fix.
candidates.answer_path: Write out what you would do after each failure, including re-entry into mechanical design.

candidates.question: What are the application deadlines for the master's, and what does waiting one more year cost you?
candidates.why: Identifies the real deadline and the cost of delay.
candidates.answer_path: Check admission calendars and ask the program whether later intakes exist.

candidates.question: Could you start the certificate now and still apply to the master's later, keeping both options open?
candidates.why: A staged route would reduce the need to decide at once.
candidates.answer_path: Ask the master's program whether certificate credits or coursework count, and check re-application rules.

candidates.question: Is there a date by which your current employer needs an answer from you, for example a project or promotion cycle that affects timing?
candidates.why: Finds whether an external deadline exists for leaving or staying.
candidates.answer_path: Check your employer's review cycle and talk to your manager about upcoming changes.

candidates.question: What is your impression that job ads require a master's based on: how many ads you have actually read, and which companies?
candidates.why: Checks the sample behind your belief.
candidates.answer_path: Count the ads you have looked at and compare with a systematic sample.

candidates.question: Where did you get the idea that a certificate may not be taken seriously: a person, a forum, or your own sense?
candidates.why: Separates evidence from impression.
candidates.answer_path: Note the source of the view and test it with two hiring managers.

candidates.question: How did you estimate what the master's would cost you, and which items did you leave out?
candidates.why: Shows whether the cost estimate is complete.
candidates.answer_path: Redo the estimate line by line with tuition, rent, insurance, and lost salary, and compare.

candidates.question: What is your estimate of how much time you could study alongside work based on, and has it held in earlier periods of studying while working?
candidates.why: Past evidence is a better guide than hope.
candidates.answer_path: Look at a past period when you combined work with study or a side project and count real hours.
